**Wednesday, February 20, 1952**

The world you arrived in was carrying winter in both hemispheres of meaning — cold season in the northern skies, and Cold War chill in every capital. Eight days before your birth, athletes had gathered in Oslo for the Winter Olympics; on the day you entered the world, they were still competing on Norwegian snow, the first Winter Games held in Scandinavia since the war had torn everything apart.

But there was something else hanging over that February. Just **fourteen days before you were born** — on February 6, 1952 — King George VI died quietly in his sleep at Sandringham. A twenty-five-year-old princess named Elizabeth learned she was Queen while on safari in Kenya, before she had even landed back in Britain. She would reign for seventy years, across your entire childhood, your adulthood, your middle age, and well into your seventies. You were born into the first hours of the longest reign in British history, and you lived almost all of it.

The world itself was barely seven years past the most destructive conflict in human history. The Soviet Union had tested its first atomic bomb in 1949; America's nuclear monopoly, itself barely a decade old, was already broken. The Korean War was grinding through its second year. The shadow of nuclear annihilation was not a metaphor. It was a genuine calculation governments made every day.

You were also born before polio had a vaccine. In the summers of 1952 and 1953, tens of thousands of American children would be infected; some would spend weeks or months in iron lungs. Jonas Salk's vaccine came in 1955, when you were three — just in time for your generation to mostly escape what prior children could not.

Now here is something remarkable. On **February 20, 1962** — your tenth birthday, exactly — John Glenn strapped himself into a capsule called Friendship 7, perched atop an Atlas rocket, and became the first American to orbit Earth. He circled the planet three times in under five hours. The nation celebrated with a kind of collective relief; America had fallen behind in the space race and desperately needed a win. You were ten years old on the day the United States finally caught up to the sky.

Twenty-four years after that, on **February 20, 1986**, the Soviet Union launched Mir — the space station that would orbit for fifteen years and host astronauts from a dozen countries. Your birthdate has been, more than once, a date the species chose to reach beyond.

And here is the broader arc. You were born before Sputnik (1957), before the first human in space (1961), before the Moon landing (1969). You arrived on a planet of roughly 2.6 billion people; today there are more than eight billion. UNIVAC I — the first commercial computer — had just been delivered to the U.S. Census Bureau the year before you were born. Television had barely entered American living rooms. Rock and roll did not yet exist as a cultural force. The Civil Rights Act was twelve years away.

In 74 years you have lived through: the complete arc of the Space Age; the Civil Rights movement; a man on the Moon; Nixon's fall; the personal computer revolution; the fall of the Berlin Wall; the Soviet Union's collapse; the internet remaking how every human being communicates; a global pandemic; and now artificial intelligence transforming the nature of knowledge work itself.

The world of February 20, 1952 was a world at the beginning of a long reckoning — with nuclear weapons, with colonial power, with racial segregation, with the limits of human reach into space. The question of whether humanity would survive these problems or be undone by them was genuinely open. The child born that Wednesday inherited all of it: the danger and the possibility, the old world still standing and the new one pressing hard against it.

What followed was one of the most compressed transformations in the history of civilization. The person born on that cold Wednesday has had a front-row seat for all of it.
